title: Productive Curiosity: The Billion Dollar Character Strength?
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. opens with Warren Buffett and Bill Gates both naming curiosity as their most important quality, and uses Gates's definition (predict, notice when the model fails, ask who to learn from) to define what he calls productive curiosity. He argues this focused, failure-owning curiosity is something every teacher should want for every student, regardless of future wealth. He then places it in the Noncognitive Factors layer of his Foundations Framework, the layer beneath curriculum and instructional method. The move is a priority argument: because lower layers matter more, teachers can cultivate productive curiosity in any classroom, high-tech or low-tech, without a curricular overhaul. He also pushes growth-mindset beliefs from head-level familiarity to heart-level operational belief.
points: Gates defines curiosity as predicting what will happen and, when the prediction fails, asking what is wrong with one's model of the world and whom to read or ask.
Productive curiosity is focused and timely, not idle wandering, and is useful to any student, worker, spouse or parent.
It sits in the Noncognitive Factors layer of the Foundations Framework, the foundation beneath the layers teachers usually debate.
Students come to believe that effort leads to improvement when classrooms let them try those beliefs out, turning mindset from head knowledge into heart-level conviction.
Any teacher can build it in any kind of classroom without a curricular overhaul.
quotes: Here is how Gates defines curiosity in the interview: “You try and predict what's gonna happen, and when it doesn't… what is it about my model of the world that's wrong? Who could I talk to, who could I read?

Is there any spouse, parent, student, or worker who wouldn't be better off with this “predict, try, analyze, learn, grow” kind of curiosity? This isn't idly wandering the Internet in search of learning: it's focused and timely — something I describe to my students as productive curiosity.
The Foundations Framework contains the essence of productive curiosity in its Noncognitive Factors layer (Figure 1) — it's the layer beneath the other two.
At the 5:08 mark, the moderator asks, “What quality has been most important for you?” They both answered with the same thing: curiosity.

And all of this can happen in any kind of classroom in the world: flashy or non-flashy, high-tech or low-tech, whole-class novels or choice-reading only, and so on. Don't confuse the top layers — the ones we tend to focus our professional development on, the ones we tend to debate in the department meetings — as the most important ones.
Every teacher can work toward making his or her students more productively curious. It need not entail a curricular overhaul.
